newsitem.title: ITALY: TENNIS-WORLD NUMBER TWO CHANG UNSTUCK BY GUMY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WORLD NUMBER TWO CHANG UNSTUCK BY GUMY.

text.p: Argentine Hernan Gumy, making a habit of upsetting top Americans on the Foro Italico's red clay, sent world number two Michael Chang crashing out of the first round of the Italian Open on Tuesday.

Gumy, whose only other victory over a world top 10 player was against Jim Courier at the same venue a year ago, brought Chang's first appearance on European clay this season to an abrupt halt with a 6-3 6-2 victory.

"It's very curious that I beat a top 10 guy one year ago and this year I beat the number two at the same tournament," said Gumy, "It makes me sure that I want to come here every year and play a top 10 player."
Chang, whose game was riddled with errors, showed sparkle only in the first game of the second set when he broke Gumy.
The Argentine number one proceeded to break the former French Open champion's serve three times.
Serving at 0-30 1-4 in the second, Chang responded to a slow hand clap by an increasingly frustrated centre court crowd with an ace and net cord to hold serve.
It was his last sign of resistance as Gumy moved him from side to side with deep, heavy top-spin drives which the lacklustre American only lobbed back.
The last point of the match summed-up Chang's day: faced with an easy kill at the net, the American let the ball go thinking it was going deep; instead it bounced just inside the baseline.
"It wasn't the best match of my career but it was probably the best win," said Gumy.

It was Chang's second successive first round loss after defeat in the American red clay court championships in Atlanta last month and suggests a disturbing dip in form before the French Open in two week's time.
Chang had dominated the hard court season winning at Hong Kong, Indian Wells and Memphis as well as the American clay court championships in Orlando.
"I don't know if it's necessarily the time zone or the surface. It's more the regular transition from hardcourt to clay," said Chang. "I don't feel as if I've made that transition yet."
Despite his defeat, Chang confessed that he felt closer than ever to being world number one.
"I feel like I'm not too far away from becoming number one, but you need to win a Grand Slam for that. If I'd won the U.S. Open last year, I'd have become number one."
Chang has been runner-up in three Grand Slam finals since his victory at the French in 1989 at the age of 17 made him the youngest ever winner of a Grand Slam tournament.
